design_detail: Narrative clinical review in JAMA Psychiatry (published title 'Neurobiology, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Methamphetamine Use Disorder: A Review'; the PMC author manuscript read here is titled 'Methamphetamine Use Disorder: The Next Addiction Crisis'). No methods section, search strategy or eligibility criteria for the narrative parts. Three themes: molecular and neural mechanisms beyond monoamine release (oxidative stress, excito- and neurotoxicity, neuroinflammation), clinical presentation with emphasis on cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, and treatment. The one quasi-systematic element is a count of ClinicalTrials.gov intervention studies containing the term 'methamphetamine' (Table 1, with an unread supplementary table). Two authors from one research institute; 94 references.
can_establish: The authors' synthesis and research agenda: which mechanisms and clinical problems they consider important, a rough audit of how many registered methamphetamine trials reported results and publications, and pointers to primary sources for prevalence, course, comorbidity, cardiovascular harm and treatment.
cannot_establish: Any of the figures it quotes (all are second-hand and must be taken from the primary sources), that methamphetamine causes the cognitive, 'degenerative' or metabolic brain states it describes (the mechanistic evidence cited is largely preclinical or in vitro, and the authors themselves say the human neurobiology is almost entirely cross-sectional), or that no medication has shown any benefit (the mirtazapine trials are not discussed).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited sources range from US surveillance (NSDUH, CDC mortality reports, ARCOS), cell and animal studies of mechanism, cross-sectional imaging and neuropsychology, single-country clinical samples (China, Taiwan, South Africa, Australia, Thailand), systematic reviews of pharmacotherapy and psychosocial treatment, and the authors' own imaging studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated for the narrative sections. For the ClinicalTrials.gov count: all registered intervention studies containing the term 'methamphetamine', with no search date, no definition of 'intervention trial' and no rule for classifying publications as showing 'no effect', 'some effect' or 'unclear' given in the text (details are in an unread supplementary table).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. Eight of the cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are from the authors' group (references 29 to 31 and 33 to 37). The treatment section does not cite either randomized trial of mirtazapine (Colfax et al., 2011; Coffin et al., published online December 2019), which bear directly on its statement that there are no pharmacological treatments.

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Forms are mentioned (ice, powder, pills) without route-specific evidence; one cited study reports a progression from first use to craving, regular use and compulsive use within about 50, 60 and 85 days in a single Chinese sample (reference 48).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only as co-use with opioids (methamphetamine as an opioid substitute or adjunct; presence of methamphetamine in opioid deaths).

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review itself notes that the scarcity of longitudinal studies makes it hard to tell whether cognitive dysfunction pre-dates use, results from it, or reflects behaviours common to substance use disorders (Biological pathways, 3rd paragraph), and that childhood adversity and pre-existing psychiatric risk are common in people with methamphetamine use disorder.

outcomes.operationalization: Not defined. 'Cognitive impairment', 'degenerative' and 'disease-modifying' are used without operational definitions.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Figures quoted second-hand: past-year methamphetamine use in people aged 12 or older up 195% from its 2010 low to 2018, 1.86 million people in the US using it in 2018 (NSDUH); age-adjusted overdose death rate involving methamphetamine more than tripled 2011 to 2016; deaths involving cocaine, amphetamines or both up 42.4%, from 12,122 (2015) to 17,258 (2016); methamphetamine present in 63% of opioid deaths; psychotic symptoms reported by 36.5% (42.7% lifetime); mood disorders 16.0%, psychotic disorders 13.0%, anxiety disorders 7.0% in one sample; moderate to severe childhood abuse or neglect 44% in one sample; more than two-thirds with cognitive impairment in one study; 5-year remission up to 30% without treatment; after treatment 61% relapse within 12 months and another 14% in years 2 to 5; 51% dropout within 2 weeks of a large programme. ClinicalTrials.gov audit (Table 1): 159 studies, 65 randomized (40.9%), 25 with results (38.5% of randomized), 14 with publications; of these 8 no effect, 3 some effect, 3 unclear; of the 11 with results but no publication, 5 no effect, 0 some effect, 6 unclear.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence selection cannot be audited. The pharmacotherapy summary relies on earlier reviews (Lee et al., 2018; Chan et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2017; German guidelines) and omits the two mirtazapine trials; the course-of-illness summary quotes relapse rates from Brecht and Herbeck (2014) but not that study's findings of frequent later abstinence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinically oriented synthesis: a list of mechanisms documented mainly in cell and animal studies; cross-sectional imaging and neuropsychological differences; second-hand epidemiological, psychiatric and cardiovascular figures from heterogeneous single samples; a registry audit in which 3 of 14 published randomized trials reported some effect; and summaries of earlier reviews showing no medication with sufficient evidence and modest evidence for contingency management and CBT.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Gaps between the review's statements and its own content: (1) the abstract says prevalence and mortality 'doubled' over 10 years, while the text gives a 195% increase in prevalence (nearly a tripling) and a more than threefold increase in methamphetamine-involved overdose death rates over 5 years; (2) a fourfold increase in methamphetamine 'consumption' is attributed to ARCOS data in a study whose cited title concerns prescription stimulants, not illicit use; (3) the conclusion states that the disorder results in significant long-term cognitive and neurological deficits and describes it as possibly degenerative, while the body calls the cognitive literature debated, notes the lack of longitudinal studies and states that the neurobiology is almost entirely cross-sectional; (4) the claim that methamphetamine puts the brain into a Warburg-type metabolic state rests on a cancer-biology reference and preclinical work; (5) exercise is said to help maintain abstinence, but the cited exercise studies measured craving, inhibitory control, depression and anxiety; (6) the statement that there are no pharmacological treatments is reasonable as regards approval, but the review does not discuss the randomized mirtazapine evidence.

timeline.event: Hart et al. critical review questioning cognitive impairment in people who use methamphetamine (cited as reference 38 for the debate)

Brecht and Herbeck: long-term relapse after treatment; this review quotes its 61% first-year relapse and 'another 14%' in years 2 to 5 (that paper's abstract says 25% and its year-by-year results sum to 15%).
Chan et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy for methamphetamine/amphetamine use disorder (cited as reference 78).
This review; Siefried et al. (2020) reach the same conclusion on pharmacotherapy from a systematic search.
McKetin et al. argue similarly that pharmacotherapy should target the wider neurobiological changes of methamphetamine use.

replication.where_it_stands: An influential agenda-setting review rather than an evidence synthesis. Its pharmacotherapy conclusion agrees with the systematic reviews read for the encyclopedia; its neurobiological framing (oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, degeneration) is a hypothesis built mostly on preclinical data, and its epidemiological figures need to be taken from primary sources.

funding.funder: The William K. Warren Foundation; National Institute on Drug Abuse (U01 DA041089); National Institute of General Medical Sciences Center Grant (1P20GM121312).
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author is an advisor to Spring Care, Inc. (a behavioural health start-up) and has received royalties for an UpToDate article about methamphetamine; no disclosures are listed for the second author.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Laureate Institute for Brain Research and the Department of Community Medicine, University of Tulsa. Several cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are the authors' own. The text read is the NIH author manuscript, whose title differs from the published title; copyedits in the published version were not checked.

what_would_settle_it: For the central neurobiological thesis: prospective human cohorts with repeated measures of neuroinflammation and oxidative-stress markers (for example TSPO PET, peripheral cytokines) and cognition across periods of use and abstinence, compared with matched people who do not use methamphetamine, and randomized trials of agents targeting these pathways with clinical outcomes (use, retention, cognition).

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria for the narrative sections; the ClinicalTrials.gov audit has a single search term, no date and no classification rules in the text.
No appraisal of the quality of cited studies; figures from single samples (China, Taiwan, South Africa) and from studies of other constructs are presented as general findings.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Eight cited imaging and relapse-prediction studies are from the authors' group; they are used for the argument about neural markers, which the review itself says are not yet clinically useful.
Preclinical mechanisms and a cancer-metabolism concept are presented as characterizing the human disorder; 'degenerative' and 'results in' are used without longitudinal human evidence.
The cognition debate is acknowledged, but positive pharmacotherapy trials (mirtazapine) and the favourable long-term course data in a cited cohort are not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); if AMSTAR 2 were applied it would fail every applicable critical item (no protocol, no described search, no list of exclusions, no appraisal of included studies) and be rated critically low. The review is useful for its research agenda, for pointers to primary sources on cardiovascular harm and for the registry audit; none of its quoted figures should be cited from it, and its mechanistic statements should be cited as hypotheses.

key_findings.finding: Past-year methamphetamine use among people aged 12 or older increased by 195% from its 2010 low to 2018, with an estimated 1.86 million people in the US using methamphetamine in 2018 (NSDUH, as cited); the age-adjusted rate of overdose deaths involving methamphetamine more than tripled from 2011 to 2016; overdose deaths involving cocaine, amphetamines or both rose 42.4%, from 12,122 in 2015 to 17,258 in 2016.
key_findings.note: The abstract summarizes these trends as a doubling of prevalence and mortality. Figures are second-hand (references 4 and 5 and NSDUH); cite the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: The review attributes a fourfold increase in methamphetamine 'consumption' between 2015 and 2016 to ARCOS data, citing a study titled as concerning prescription stimulants (reference 3).
key_findings.note: This figure does not describe illicit methamphetamine use and should not be cited as such.

key_findings.finding: Course after treatment, as quoted from Brecht and Herbeck (2014): 61% relapse within the first 12 months and another 14% during years 2 to 5; without treatment, 5-year remission up to 30% (Lanyon et al., 2019).
key_findings.note: The source paper's abstract gives 25% for years 2 to 5 and its results sum to 15%; the review omits that source's findings of later abstinence in most people who relapsed.

key_findings.finding: Psychiatric figures as quoted: psychotic symptoms in 36.5% of people using methamphetamine (42.7% lifetime; reference 50, a meta-analysis titled as concerning substance-induced psychotic disorder); co-occurring mood 16.0%, psychotic 13.0% and anxiety 7.0% disorders in one sample (reference 55); moderate to severe childhood abuse or neglect 44% in one sample (reference 53).

Cognition: the review states that the effect of methamphetamine on cognition is debated and that the lack of longitudinal studies prevents separating pre-existing from drug-related dysfunction, then concludes that methamphetamine is associated with moderate dysfunction in several cognitive processes; more than two-thirds of people with methamphetamine use disorder are said to show cognitive impairment on the basis of one study (reference 43).
key_findings.locator: Biological Pathways, Neural Basis and Cognition, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine is said to be present in 63% of opioid deaths, citing a CDC report on 25 states, July 2017 to June 2018 (reference 73).
key_findings.note: Not verified against the source; take the figure and its denominator from the MMWR report.

key_findings.finding: ClinicalTrials.gov audit (term 'methamphetamine'): 159 registered studies; 65 randomized (40.9%); 25 of those with results (38.5%); 14 with identifiable publications, of which 8 reported no effect, 3 some effect and 3 effects not bearing on efficacy; of the 11 with results but no publication, 5 no effect, none some effect, 6 unclear.
key_findings.note: No search date or classification rules in the text; the trial list is in an unread supplementary table.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacotherapy, second-hand: a systematic review of 49 studies of 20 medications found limited evidence of benefit for methylphenidate, bupropion, modafinil and naltrexone but none sufficient for routine use (reference 75); anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, opioid antagonists, varenicline and atomoxetine showed low-strength or insufficient evidence on abstinence of 3 or more weeks (reference 78). The review concludes there is not sufficient evidence that medications by themselves are useful.

Psychosocial treatment, second-hand: in a network meta-analysis of cocaine and amphetamine addiction, only contingency management plus community reinforcement increased end-of-treatment abstinence over treatment as usual (reference 81); brief CBT reduced use frequency and severity in one trial in methadone patients; behavioural activation was beneficial in 7 of 8 studies across several substances; exercise studies reported reduced craving and improved inhibitory control, depression and anxiety. 51% dropped out within 2 weeks in one large pooled dataset of pharmacotherapy trials (reference 89).

Mechanistic thesis: beyond monoamine release, methamphetamine engages oxidative stress, neuro- and excitotoxicity and neuroinflammation (including TLR4 binding and inflammasome activation in microglia), which the authors argue amount to an altered brain state resembling degenerative CNS disease and a Warburg-type metabolic shift.
key_findings.locator: Biological Pathways, Neural Basis and Cognition, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Supported in the text mainly by cell, animal and cancer-biology references (references 10 to 22); presented by the editors as the authors' hypothesis.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the neurobiology of the disorder is almost entirely derived from cross-sectional studies, and that imaging markers used to predict relapse have not yet proved clinically useful.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion and Relevance, last part; Biological Pathways, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease is presented as the most severe medical problem and the leading cause of death in methamphetamine use disorder (reference 66). Methamphetamine-related strokes are said to be rising, to occur most often in young men and to be primarily haemorrhagic (67); methamphetamine is associated with vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, atherosclerotic plaque formation, cardiac arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy (68); the associated cardiomyopathy is described as left ventricular dilatation with impaired ejection fraction and raised tissue markers of inflammation and fibrosis (69, 70), and the electrocardiogram as frequently showing tachyarrhythmias, right axis deviation, left ventricular hypertrophy, P pulmonale, inferior Q waves, lateral T wave inversion and a longer QTc interval (71); symptoms preceding death attributed solely to methamphetamine toxicity are given as collapse, breathing difficulty and hyperthermia (72).
key_findings.note: All of it is second-hand, and two of the inferences do not follow from the sources cited. The leading-cause-of-death statement rests on a 10-year follow-up study of cardiovascular and stroke risk, which estimates risk and does not establish what people who use methamphetamine most often die of. The statement that strokes are primarily haemorrhagic rests on a review of published cases, which reflects what gets reported rather than relative incidence; the same inference is recorded on sc_hemphill_2024. Every figure and description here must be taken from the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says prevalence and mortality doubled over the past 10 years; the text gives a 195% increase in past-year use from 2010 to 2018 and a more than threefold rise in the methamphetamine overdose death rate from 2011 to 2016.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline trend is stated inconsistently; claims about trends must come from NSDUH and CDC sources directly, with years and measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'fourfold increase in methamphetamine consumption' is cited to ARCOS via a study of prescription stimulant trends.
reporting_issues.consequence: A prescription-distribution figure is presented in the context of an illicit-drug crisis; it should not be cited for illicit use.

reporting_issues.issue: The relapse figure for years 2 to 5 after treatment (14%) attributed to Brecht and Herbeck (2014) matches neither that paper's abstract (25%) nor its year-by-year results (15%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Secondary quotation drift; the primary paper's results section is the source to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: Several cited sources concern different constructs from the statements they support: a meta-analysis of substance-induced psychotic disorder for 'psychotic symptoms'; a network meta-analysis of cocaine and amphetamine addiction for 'MUD patients'; a pooled analysis of pharmacotherapy trials for dropout from 'intervention programs'; a review of 49 studies called a meta-analysis; and the 42.4% rise in overdose deaths from 12,122 in 2015 to 17,258 in 2016 is cited to a report titled for drug overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants with abuse potential, 2003 to 2017, while the sentence reads cocaine, amphetamines, or both substances combined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each figure must be re-anchored in its primary source before use.

reporting_issues.issue: The Interventions section gives the registry address as 'clinicialtrials.gov' and contains a garbled sentence on the number of Phase II studies in the cited review ('35 studies related to 33 Phase II quality').
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the counts from the cited review cannot be relied on as quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC text is the accepted author manuscript, whose title (Methamphetamine Use Disorder: The Next Addiction Crisis) differs from the published title recorded by the first reader from PubMed (Neurobiology, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment of Methamphetamine Use Disorder: A Review). The author-manuscript title is confirmed from the saved page; the published title could not be re-checked in this reading, which had no access to PubMed or the publisher, so that half of the issue remains single-reader.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors refer to the author manuscript; wording may differ slightly in the published version, so the reference record should use the Crossref title.

reporting_issues.issue: Two causal-sounding generalizations rest on single studies. Clinical Presentation ¶1 reports that the transition from casual to compulsive use takes on average about 50 days to first craving, 60 days to regular use and 85 days to compulsive use, from one sample (reference 48). Clinical Presentation ¶2 reports that rising adolescent cannabis use may increase the probability of initiating other illicit drugs including methamphetamine through biological and social processes, from one longitudinal study (61), offered as evidence for the gateway hypothesis (62).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither can be cited from this review as a general pattern. The day counts need their primary sample, population and measurement before use, and the gateway sentence is a single longitudinal association presented as a mechanism.

Published title and abstract checked on PubMed (PMID 32267484).
